title: Synchronous and asynchronous
summary: Request-reply chains multiply failure; queues decouple it. Know the numbers and the trade-offs.

steps.title: Request-reply: everyone waits
body: In a **synchronous** (request-reply) integration the caller waits while the integration calls each backend.
consumer ──► gateway ──► integration ──► orders ──► warehouse ──► billing
◄────────────── one answer, after all of them ──────────────
Two consequences follow, and every architect should be able to compute them:
- **Latency adds up**: sequential calls of 40 ms, 120 ms and 80 ms take at least 240 ms. Calls made in
parallel take as long as the slowest one.
- **Availability multiplies**: if each of three services is up 99% of the time, the chain is up
`0.99 × 0.99 × 0.99 ≈ 97%`. Add services and it only gets worse.

code: foreach (var a in up) chain *= a;
steps.explain: Three 99% services in a row give about 97%: roughly 22 hours of downtime a month instead of about 7 for one of them.

steps.title: Asynchronous: accept now, finish later
body: In an **asynchronous** integration the caller hands over the work and does not wait for it to finish:
(order placed on a queue; the warehouse and billing process it when they can)
- The consumer stays up when the warehouse is down: the message waits on the queue.
- The price: the answer is **eventually consistent**, the consumer needs a status endpoint, a callback or an
event, and messages can be **delivered more than once**, so consumers must be idempotent (module 2).
- **Fire-and-forget** is the extreme: no reply at all (an audit event, a notification).

items: Show a book's price on the product page
Check stock while the customer waits at checkout
Send the order to the warehouse for picking
Tell analytics a book was viewed
Validate a discount code as the user types it

steps.prompt: Match each style to what the consumer gets back.
pairs: `200 OK` with the answer, after every backend has replied
An acknowledgement that the message was queued, and nothing more
Later, a call to a URL the consumer registered

steps.prompt: `POST /orders` synchronously calls the order service, the warehouse, billing and the carrier. The carrier is down for 10 minutes. What happens, and what is the better design?
options: Every order fails for 10 minutes; accept the order (202), store it, and book the carrier asynchronously with retries
Nothing; HTTP retries hide the outage
Only the carrier step fails, the rest succeed silently
The gateway's rate limit protects the carrier, so orders still succeed
steps.explain: In a synchronous chain the least available service sets the availability of the whole operation. A queue lets the carrier catch up when it returns.
`202 Accepted` says the request was taken but not finished. `Location` tells the client where to check progress. `201 Created` would claim the order already exists in its final form.

steps.title: Chain arithmetic
prompt: - `double ChainAvailability(double[] availabilities)`: the availability of a synchronous chain (the product). An empty chain is `1.0`.
- `int SequentialLatencyMs(int[] latencies)`: total when the calls happen one after another.
- `int ParallelLatencyMs(int[] latencies)`: total when all calls start together and you wait for all of them. An empty array is `0`.
solution: foreach (var a in availabilities) result *= a;
hints: Start the product at `1.0` and multiply.
LINQ's `Sum()` and `Max()` do the latency; guard the empty array for `Max()`.
